metric.why: Rates rising after a decade of decline is the clearest market evidence that demand outran supply. Rate data is compiled by commercial research firms listed in the directory below; it is not republished here.
metric.definition: Market rate per kilowatt per month for leased capacity, the price signal for scarcity in each metro.

reading.body:
Colocation rental rates are the price signal for data center scarcity, and their reversal after a decade of decline is the clearest market evidence that demand outran supply.

The metric is the monthly price of a kilowatt of leased capacity in a given metro. That makes it a direct read on the cost of the two things AI scaling actually consumes at the site level: power and the building that houses it. Capital expenditure and equipment lead times, the two sibling metrics, describe what operators are spending and how long they wait. Rental rates describe what the market pays for capacity that already exists, which is why a turn from falling to rising prices carries more information than either of the others alone. A decade of decline meant supply could keep ahead of demand. The reversal means it no longer can, at least in the markets where the rate is measured.

The data does not include the rates themselves. It states the direction of travel and the definition, and it notes that the underlying figures are compiled by commercial research firms rather than carried here. So there is no level, no year over year percentage, no list of metros, and no indication of how uneven the rise is across markets. Rates are also a per metro measure, which means a broad trend can conceal markets where capacity is still cheap and others where it is acutely short. Nothing here establishes how much of the increase is power cost, land, construction, or pure scarcity rent.

What the metric does establish is where to look for confirmation. If compute demand is the upstream force and buildings and power are the binding constraint, the constraint should appear as price in the markets that lease capacity, not only as backlog in equipment orders or as rising capital budgets. Rental rates are the place that shows up first and most legibly, because they are set by transactions rather than by plans.
